analysis.one_liner: Takes landing slots from dominant airlines at four crowded airports and auctions them to new competitors to lower fares.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its aviation subcommittee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: At the four busiest, slot-controlled airports (LaGuardia, JFK, O'Hare, and Reagan National), a handful of dominant airlines hold most of the takeoff and landing rights, which limits competition and keeps fares high. The bill would have the Transportation Secretary take up to 10 percent of a dominant carrier's slots at these airports and auction them to new entrant and smaller airlines, restrict the use of 40 percent of the redistributed slots for flights to underserved airports, speed up federal review of complaints that big carriers are pricing competitors out, and let passengers sue airlines under state consumer laws despite federal preemption.
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers flying to and from the four high-density airports, who could see more carriers and lower fares, and new or smaller airlines that would gain access to slots they otherwise could not obtain. Communities served by low-competition airports would also gain, since a share of redistributed slots must serve flights to those airports.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Air travelers and new low-cost airlines

how_it_helps.text: If demand for slots at a high-density airport exceeds supply, the Secretary must withdraw up to 10 percent of a dominant carrier's slots (5 percent in later rounds) and auction them to new entrant and limited incumbent carriers, which is designed to add competitors and pressure fares down [S2][S3].

40 percent of redistributed slots at each airport (10 percent at JFK) must be set aside for flights between the airport and low-competition airports, underserved markets with fewer flights or above-average fares [S3].

The Secretary must resolve all pending complaints alleging predatory practices by airlines within 6 to 9 months, act on new complaints within 30 days, and enjoin practices found predatory after a hearing [S2][S3].

The bill amends federal preemption law so private parties can sue airlines under state common law or state statutes to enforce their rights, opening a legal avenue that federal aviation law currently bars [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant airlines holding 10 percent or more of the slots at LaGuardia, JFK, O'Hare, or Reagan National, which would lose up to 10 percent of their slots at those airports (though they could be reimbursed from auction proceeds for investments in withdrawn slots), plus airlines that benefit from the current slot scarcity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dominant incumbent airlines at the four airports

drawbacks.text: Forcing dominant carriers to give up slots, even with reimbursement for investments, is a mandated redistribution of valuable property; incumbents would argue it punishes carriers that built up their schedules and could reduce service on some routes [S3].

The bill prohibits treating slots as assets for collateral or bankruptcy purposes, which could disrupt airline financing and already-existing agreements, since it does not apply to agreements in effect at enactment but would affect new financing going forward [S3].

The Secretary has discretion in determining demand, identifying dominant carriers, and defining predatory practices, so the actual number of slots redistributed and the pace of enforcement depend heavily on administrative choices rather than automatic rules [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-documented problem: landing slots at the four high-density airports are dominated by a few carriers, limiting competition and keeping fares high. The core mechanism (auctioning a capped share of incumbent slots to new entrants, with some slots reserved for underserved routes) is a measured approach, and reimbursement for investments softens the blow to incumbents. The main honest caveats are that outcomes depend on the Secretary's discretionary determinations and that incumbents lose valuable property rights. The bill died without any committee consideration, so its actual effects were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then sent to its aviation subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Louise Slaughter introduced the Airline Competition and Lower Fares Act on January 6, 1999, the first day of the 106th Congress [S1][S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, the committee with jurisdiction over aviation [S5].
On January 19, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a Democrat, and the Congress ended January 3, 2001, without the bill ever reaching the House floor [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant airlines holding most slots at LaGuardia, JFK, O'Hare, and Reagan National kept their slots and the pricing power that comes with them. Air travelers at those airports continued to face limited competition and the fares that go with it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant incumbent airlines at the four airports

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill; it was sponsored and cosponsored by two House Democrats, and neither party as a bloc ever weighed in on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have taken up to 10 percent of a dominant carrier's slots at LaGuardia, JFK, O'Hare, and Reagan National for auction to competitors, directly reducing the market power that slot hoarding provides. Because the bill died, these carriers kept both their slots and the scarce-access economics that sustain higher fares.

The bill would have created the only realistic way for new and small carriers to acquire slots at the four high-density airports, since auctions are limited to new entrants and limited incumbents and resold slots stay within that class. Their gain would have been passengers' gain in the form of more competition.
A fixed share of redistributed slots must be used for flights to underserved airports, which would have expanded service to places with limited flights or above-average fares.
